thread.title: God or Man?

author: Bill Muehlenberg
title: God or Man?
text:
On divine sovereignty and human responsibility:
Sometimes even television commercials can contain some much-needed wisdom. That includes the old taco ad that used to run. As I said in another piece about it: “Adults are arguing and debating about which must be used: soft or hard taco shells. A little girl rightly asks, ‘Why not both?’ Why not indeed! It is a false dilemma to demand one or the other when both can do.” https://billmuehlenberg.com/2024/01/02/why-not-both/
Of course taco preferences are not all that important. But in that article I went on to look at four pairs of biblical truths regarding the Christian life which no man should put asunder:
-Evangelism or social action
-Love or obedience
-Daily reading or deep study
-Faith or works
In each of these matters the Bible insists on asking: Why not both? And this goes for the really hardcore theological debates such as the one being discussed here. Indeed, the questions raised by the terms found in my subtitle have exercised the finest theological, biblical and philosophical minds for millennia.
And at times the discussion can result in real polarisation, since some parties will emphasise one side and play down the other, and vice versa. But Scripture does not allow that: it fully emphasises and affirms both realities, and we should too. Sure, it might seem that to affirm one is to negate the other. But that is not the case.
What we must admit is that there is certainly some mystery here, and legitimate questions can and do arise. After all, we are all mere men – fallen, finite and fallible creatures – who are trying to understand Almighty God. That is something we will never fully achieve – at least in this life. So the best we can do is let Scripture speak and try to get our heads around that.
With so many biblical texts declaring the sovereignty of God, and so many texts declaring how humans are morally accountable and responsible for their choices, all we can do is declare both, and believe that they do indeed stand together.
And so often that is just what Scripture does. Hundreds of passages state the one truth, and hundreds of passages state the other. And what is of real interest is how often both biblical truths are found together in the same passage or even in the same sentence.
The biblical writers – led by the Holy Spirit – were not afraid to do this, and therefore we should be willing to fully embrace both sets of biblical truths and believe that they can and do go together. We do NOT need to choose one and discard the other. That is a false dilemma. We are to run with both, simultaneously.
With all this in mind, let me offer just four remarkable examples of this. And I deal with what involves one of the most important and heavy-duty examples of human choices coalescing with the purposes of God. They involve the most incredible and profound activity of all time: the death and resurrection of our Lord.
All are found in the opening chapters of the book of Acts. All four of these were spoken by the Apostle Peter. And all four so very clearly demonstrate that the Bible teaches that God is indeed achieving his purposes and is in control, but also that humans are indeed held accountable for the choices that they have made. Here they are:
Acts 2:22-23 Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.
Acts 3:13-19 The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. “And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out…
Acts 4:27-28 Indeed Herod and Pontius Pilate met together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel in this city to conspire against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed. They did what your power and will had decided beforehand should happen.
Acts 5:30-32 The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.
Here it is affirmed that human beings (be they Roman rulers or Jewish leaders) were certainly responsible for the death of Jesus. But in each case Peter insists that this was something fully part of the divine plan. It was not an accident or some last-minute decision: Jesus was “delivered up by God’s set plan and foreknowledge” (Acts 2:23).
Again, a million questions can arise here. How can this be? Needless to say, an ocean of ink has been spilled on this over the centuries. Plenty of useful answers have been given that seek to affirm both truths and how they can logically and morally cohere.
Obviously I cannot here even begin to share the tiniest fraction of those. But I can do two things. One, I can alert you to a very small collection of helpful books on these matters. While this piece was penned 15 years ago, and only contains 45 recommended volumes (out of so many), it does give you a number of leads as to where to go for further reading and reflection on these mega-issues: https://billmuehlenberg.com/2011/11/28/readings-in-divine-sovereignty-and-human-responsibility/
It should be noted that I highlighted one volume from that list: Divine Sovereignty and Human Responsibility by D. A. Carson. I still think that is one of the better books to begin with if you have not yet waded into these deep theological and biblical waters.
Divine Sovereignty and Human Responsibility by D. A. Carson
The other thing I can do is offer just a very few comments by others (out of kazillions) that might be of help to some people (or rattle the minds even further of some others!). Here are a few brief but nonetheless useful quotes:
“In the Bible, divine sovereignty and human responsibility are not enemies. They are not uneasy neighbors; they are not in an endless state of cold war with each other. They are friends, and they work together.” J. I. Packer
“I never try to reconcile friends.” Charles Spurgeon (when asked how he might reconcile these two truths)
“Just because God is sovereign doesn’t mean you can lean on your shovel and pray for a hole.” Unknown
“The truth is not in the middle, and not in one extreme, but in both extremes.” Rev Charles Simeon
“The real inter-relation between God’s omnipotence and Man’s freedom is something we can’t find out. Looking at the Sheep & the Goats every man can be quite sure that every kind act he does will be accepted by Christ. Yet, equally, we all do feel sure that all the good in us comes from Grace. We have to leave it at that. I find the best plan is to take the Calvinist view of my own virtues and other people’s vices: and the other view of my own vices and other people’s virtues.” C. S. Lewis
“Pray as though everything depended on God. Work as though everything depended on you.” Augustine
“The Bible teaches me the sovereignty of God and, equally definitely, it teaches me the duty of prayer. I hold to that doctrine, teaching, and I pray. I am not concerned with reconciling them. I cannot. Nobody else can. I imagine that in glory we shall be given the explanation.” Dr Martyn Lloyd-Jones
“We must be careful not to so zealously maintain the sovereignty of God that we end up denying human freedom and responsibility. At the same time we must be careful not to so zealously preserve human freedom that we reduce God to an impotent spectator of world affairs.” R. C. Sproul
“God is absolutely sovereign, but his sovereignty never functions in Scripture to reduce human responsibility. Human beings are responsible creatures—that is, they choose, they believe, they disobey, they respond, and there is moral significance in their choices; however, human responsibility never functions in Scripture to diminish God’s sovereignty or to make God absolutely contingent.” D. A. Carson
“The same event, the death of Jesus, is attributed simultaneously to the purpose of God and to the wickedness of men.” John Stott (on Acts 2:23)
If the most momentous event in human history can be declared to be the result of both God’s purposes and human choices, then we should be willing to see this divine/human interplay in other areas of life. To do so will not mean all of our questions will be answered, but it does mean we will be seeking to be fully biblical.
[1615 words]
